title: Canada holds as an energy shock interrupts disinflation and weakens the growth outlook
summary: The Bank of Canada held its overnight target at 2.25% on 18 March, with a 2.50% Bank Rate and a 2.20% deposit rate. February inflation and the domestic activity data by themselves would have pointed towards less inflation pressure than the Bank had expected. The outbreak of war in the Middle East changed the information set. Gasoline prices were already responding to higher oil prices, global financial conditions had tightened and shipping disruptions threatened input supplies. Governing Council judged the risks to growth tilted down even as risks to inflation rose. The unchanged rate preserved flexibility while these risks were moving in opposite directions.

The weakness in Canadian GDP required interpretation. The economy expanded 2.4% in the third quarter of 2025 then contracted 0.6% in the fourth quarter. The fourth-quarter decline exceeded the Bank’s January expectation largely because firms ran down inventories more than anticipated. Domestic demand nonetheless grew more than 2%, supported by consumption and government expenditure, while housing remained weak. A firm can meet current orders by selling earlier production, which reduces measured output without an equivalent decline in current sales. The inventory result therefore carried less evidence of a collapse in underlying demand than the GDP headline suggested. Labour and trade indicators gave independent reasons for caution. Employment gains made late in 2025 had largely reversed in January and February, unemployment had risen to 6.7% in February, and exports looked weak beneath the volatility (domestic activity paragraphs).

The February inflation figures primarily describe conditions before higher energy costs had fully reached retail prices. Headline inflation fell from 2.3% in January to 1.8% in February. Inflation adjusted for changes in indirect taxes and the Bank’s core measures were all close to 2%. Food inflation had slowed while remaining elevated. The subsequent rise in gasoline therefore pointed to a near-term increase in headline CPI even without any intensification of domestic demand. It would take additional evidence on the persistence and breadth of price changes to infer an enduring departure from price stability. The March statement neither quantified the peak in inflation nor estimated the net effect of the conflict on Canadian GDP.

The external transmission could extend well beyond fuel. The Bank identified the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz and the possibility of disruptions to fertilizer and other commodities. Higher energy costs could thus reach households directly through fuel and later through production or transport costs. At the same time global bond yields had risen, equities had fallen and credit spreads had widened. These shifts could tighten the financing conditions faced by Canadian borrowers even though the domestic policy target stayed unchanged. The Canadian dollar was relatively stable against the US dollar over the period the statement describes. Country-specific currency pressure was therefore a less obvious immediate explanation for the higher gasoline prices than the jump in global energy costs. Relative stability of the bilateral exchange rate says little about the exchange rate against other trading partners.

The release’s global growth reference also has a time boundary. The Bank said the world economy had been on track for around 3% growth before the war. It did not reaffirm 3% as a new conditional estimate after the shock. The US economy had continued to benefit from consumption and AI-related investment, while recent Canadian data suggested weaker near-term growth than in January as firms adjusted to US tariffs. The Council’s decision left open how those forces would develop alongside the energy shock. To measure the financial-market response to the announcement itself, the relevant comparison would be Canadian rates before and after the release, accounting for concurrent oil and foreign-rate moves. The broad asset moves discussed by the Bank describe the preceding period.

questions.question: How much of the domestic slowdown survived the inventory adjustment?
questions.detail: Decompose real GDP into final domestic demand, inventories and net trade, then compare subsequent production, sales and employment in sectors most affected by tariffs. If inventories were rebuilt into stable orders, output could recover without a substantial improvement in final demand. Continued weakness in hours and export volumes would place a different weight on the GDP decline.

questions.question: Did higher energy prices alter underlying inflation or only the near-term headline path?
questions.detail: Track gasoline separately from energy-intensive transport and food inputs, then examine the breadth of non-energy price increases and expectations at multiple horizons. Timing is critical because February CPI predates much of the shock. A rise in fuel prices alongside stable core breadth would present a different decision from sustained pass-through with rising longer-run expectations.

questions.question: How much of the tightening in Canadian financial conditions was imported?
questions.detail: Match the timing of oil, US and Canadian yields, risk spreads and the bilateral currency around the conflict news and around the Bank’s announcement separately. An unchanged target can coincide with tighter borrowing conditions as global yields and spreads rise. Comparing horizons and event windows would help distinguish international repricing from a change in the expected Canadian policy path.
